Why Radar selected it

2,629 → 2,632public employee profiles · +3 in 1h27m
5,763 → 5,767public shifts · +4 in the same window
+150 blocks24,507,088 → 24,507,238 removed on the server counter

The server dashboard moved during two Radar checks, and a creator post in r/WebGames had 26 votes with comments describing 30–40 minute and multi-hour sessions. A weekly r/incremental_games discussion independently recommended it as a calm shared persistent-multiplayer experience. Together, those signals justified recording the onboarding and first economic cycle.

Counterpoint. This was a short observation window. CCU moved from 1 to 0, peak CCU was 19, and an earlier snapshot showed one leaderboard player responsible for roughly 16.86 million blocks. Public server counters are first-party operational data, not independent analytics, and the active population may be narrow.

The pitch works because the goal is absurdly larger than one player

The landing page does not lead with a list of mining features. It states a company mandate: remove all 999 billion blocks of the planet. The remaining percentage barely changes, and the estimated completion date stretches absurdly far into the future. That scale turns a small personal action into participation in a public monument. Company reports, a damage map, personnel files, graves, leaderboards, and active-site codes all reinforce the idea that other people were here before you.

1Choose an active site and begin a shift
2Dig materials until the pack is full
3Reach a surface store or risk burial
4Sell the pack and buy capacity or speed
5Return deeper and add to global progress

Moment-to-moment play: aim at voxel blocks and click or hold to dig. The Handbook states that deeper material pays better, from coal and copper through iron, silver, gold, amethyst, and diamond. The basic pack imposes a hard return point; the basic shovel defines labour speed; torches, ladder rungs, flares, dynamite, and later equipment extend how deep and safely a shift can continue.

Controls observed: WASD movement, mouse look, click/hold to dig, Space to jump, 1–9 or mouse wheel to select the hotbar, E/right-click to use an item, B for the Company Store, Tab for the board, ? for the Handbook, T for expressions, and hold K to bury yourself.

Surface economy: a full pack must be hauled to a surface store—or eventually a deployed outpost—before it can be sold. The initial store prices shown were $60 for the first shovel upgrade, $50 for the first backpack upgrade, and $15 for five torches; ladder rungs, flares, storage, insurance, and outposts open longer-term spending paths.

Persistence and death: the claim code keeps a profile across devices and a world code lets friends converge on a site. The Handbook warns that a 10 m fall turns the screen red and a 15 m fall buries the employee with everything. Death removes all equipment, issues a fresh permit, and leaves the entire fortune in a real grave block that anyone can dig up.

Progression beyond equipment

  • Job signs issue contracts in sets of three
  • Completing a set pays a bonus and refreshes it
  • Completed contracts raise corporate rank
  • Recruiting links can satisfy hiring contracts
  • Promotion unlocks dynamite clearance
  • Storage crates create underground cash-out points
  • Insurance cancels one accident, then premiums rise
  • Personnel files preserve lifetime output and graves

The first-session path

00:00–00:50

The player inspects the Company Report, Damage Map, personnel surfaces, Telegram link, and the live global block count before starting.

00:50–01:09

A lightweight registration creates an employee name and claim code. The world-code field offers a direct way to land with friends.

01:09–01:58

The first-person shift begins underground. The player digs mixed materials, reaches 30/30 pack capacity, and receives a surface-sale instruction.

01:58–03:57

The store cannot be opened underground. Holding K intentionally buries the character with the full fortune; a later fatal fall demonstrates the same grave rule involuntarily. Each death removes equipment, issues a fresh permit, and leaves recoverable coordinates. A new shift introduces torches and approved workplace expressions.

04:22–06:39

The player reaches the large surface quarry, searches the Handbook and Personnel File, but still struggles to identify exactly where the sale interaction is available.

06:39–10:23

Money and a fresh shift are recovered; ladders and another player are visible. Navigation back to the precise surface-store state takes several minutes and includes camera/performance friction.

10:23–12:32

The Company Store finally opens. The player sells, buys shovel and backpack upgrades, returns underground, fills the larger pack, sells again, and confirms the repeatable loop.

What gives the grind meaning

The world remembers labour

Excavation is not reset between runs. Old tunnels, huge open pits, graves, ladders, and signs make anonymous activity tangible even when no other player is currently nearby.

Corporate fiction unifies the UI

Company reports, forms, ranks, personnel files, “approved expressions,” and blunt labour language turn menus into worldbuilding instead of neutral utilities.

Death creates stories, not only loss

A grave records a place, fortune, and cause. Anyone can recover it, creating rescue, theft, griefing, and shareable coordinates from one simple rule; insurance later offers exactly one protected accident.

Progress is personal and planetary

The HUD shows both “you removed” and the global remainder. A tiny session therefore advances equipment and a public project at the same time.

Where the first session breaks rhythm

The first sale is a navigation test

The pack-full message says B works “at the surface,” but reaching terrain with depth 0 did not immediately communicate whether the store was available. The player spent several minutes testing keys and routes.

Essential rules are documentation-first

The Handbook is comprehensive, but the dig–sell transition, burial consequences, and surface/outpost distinction matter before a new player is likely to open a long reference panel.

Darkness obscures affordance

The visual tone is distinctive, yet surface silhouettes, paths, interactable structures, and terrain edges can collapse into the same near-black values—especially at night.

Movement instability is costly near drops

The recording noted abrupt camera turns and lag while navigating ladders and ledges. In a game where death can bury the entire fortune, control instability amplifies perceived unfairness.

Recommendations

1 · Create a first-shift contract

Use one short objective chain: remove 10 blocks → fill the pack → follow a visible beacon to a store → sell → buy one upgrade → return. Retire it once completed.

2 · Make store access binary

Replace the small helper line with a clear HUD state: “STORE LOCKED · 14m below surface” or “STORE READY · press B.” A surface beacon should identify the valid zone.

3 · Explain burial before the hold

When K begins charging, state exactly what will happen: equipment lost, full fortune placed in a public grave, and recovery available at these coordinates.

4 · Show contribution after every sale

Pair cash with a planetary receipt: personal blocks this shift, share of site output, materials delivered, and the global counter delta while the player was active.

5 · Improve night readability

Raise local contrast around climbable geometry, stores, paths, and other players without flattening the dark atmosphere. Functional light should communicate routes as well as mood.

6 · Convert persistence into return prompts

On exit, summarize the grave or current dig site, the next affordable upgrade, and activity since the last shift. The world already remembers; the UI should make that memory actionable.

The public landing page leads with the ‘remove the planet’ premise, a global counter, world/player statistics, and clear entry/account actions.

The 3D voxel world fills the viewport; crosshair remains central. Depth, money, pack, site population, personal output, global progress, and hotbar live at the periphery.

Surface and personnel layer

Overlays & interruptions

  • Landing statistics and employee/world-code setup.
  • Company Store categories with upgrade comparisons.
  • Employee Handbook and Personnel File document panels.
  • Pack-full prompt, death/respawn interruption, and tombstone recovery state.

Motion, VFX & feedback

  • Voxel targeting and multiple crack stages culminate in particles, sound, and material pickup.
  • Depth lighting darkens progressively; torches/flares create local falloff and a strong placed-light response.
  • Pack gain/sale, tool upgrade, and personal/global progress use distinct counters and deltas.
  • Fall/damage, death, respawn, and tombstone recovery need readable transitions without disorienting camera motion.
  • Remote employees and persistent placed objects update smoothly while visibly exposing connection/stale state.

Responsive, accessibility & edge cases

  • The site claims mobile support, so digging, hotbar selection, movement, jump, placement, and panel close all require explicit touch equivalents.
  • Offer brightness/gamma, reduced head-bob, FOV, sensitivity, flash, and motion settings for a dark first-person game.
  • Never make a claim/world code readable only once; provide copy, recovery guidance, and clear privacy warning.
  • Server disconnect, full pack, invalid placement, death, duplicate recovery, and global-counter staleness need distinct recoverable states.
Reconstruction test. A new employee must join or share a world, dig and identify a material, fill and sell a pack, buy/equip an upgrade, place a traversal/light object, read account statistics, die, locate and reclaim the tombstone fortune, and distinguish personal, site, and planet-wide progress.

Creator context · verified public sources

Developer dossier

Who made H.O.L.E., the public context around the work, and the nearest verified projects. Private identity, location, employment, and credits are left unknown unless the creator or an official project page states them.

Public identity and credit

H.O.L.E. is publicly presented by the creator handle Pergamum_. The creator describes it as a free hobby project built around one persistent planet that every employee can dig. No verified real name or studio entity was located.

Location and working context

No city, country, employer, or formal team was verified. The creator says the project runs on one small server; that describes infrastructure scale, not personal location.

Timeline

A developer post on 23 August 2026 introduced the persistent shared-world premise. A precise standalone release date was not verified, so this dossier keeps the dated public post and the 15 September recording separate from any inferred launch date.

Other verified work

No other shipped games were verified from the official site and linked creator profile at research time. H.O.L.E., its stats surface, and the related development discussion are the complete attributable public product set used here.

Visible development pattern

The project’s visible priority is a social systems hook achieved with deliberately small infrastructure: persistent digging, personal and global contribution, recoverable death wealth, upgrade economy, and shareable world codes.

What this means for the teardown

The small-server disclosure is important for reconstruction risk. Treat global counters, persistence, ownership/claim codes, tombstone recovery, and concurrency as core product systems with explicit stale/error states—not just HUD decoration.

Identity boundary. Pergamum_ remains a public handle. The dossier does not attempt to deanonymize the creator or infer location, release history, or team composition where the official sources are silent.

04
Reconstruction blueprint

What must exist to rebuild the observed game

This is a product and systems specification derived from the public build and the recorded first session. It describes observable behaviour, not the original source-code architecture.

Reconstruction confidence. High for registration, basic controls, materials, pack limit, death/graves, surface selling, and first upgrades. Medium for contracts, outposts, insurance, ranks, dynamite, and server-scale persistence.

State machineSession flow

  • Landing / world context → inspect company report, damage map, server statistics, and the planetary objective.
  • Employee registration → choose a name/world code and receive a cross-device claim code.
  • Shift spawn → enter a persistent site with equipment, empty pack, depth, and global progress HUD.
  • Excavate → damage voxel blocks, collect materials by depth/value, and stop when capacity is full.
  • Surface / outpost sale → convert carried material into cash.
  • Store / contracts → buy tools and fulfil three-job sets for rank progression.
  • Death or self-burial → lose equipment, create a public grave containing the fortune, and respawn with a fresh permit.

Input contractControls

  • WASD moves, mouse looks, click/hold digs, and Space jumps.
  • 1–9 or the wheel selects hotbar items; E/right-click uses the selected item.
  • B opens the Company Store only from a valid surface/outpost state; Tab opens the board; ? opens the Handbook.
  • T opens approved expressions; holding K intentionally buries the employee.

Rules engineSimulation and resolution

  • Voxel blocks persist globally after removal and feed both personal and planetary counters.
  • Deeper material pays more: the Handbook ranges from coal/copper through iron, silver, gold, amethyst, and diamond.
  • The backpack is a hard collection cap and the shovel controls labour speed.
  • A ten-metre fall warns with a red screen; a fifteen-metre fall can bury the player with all equipment and fortune.
  • A grave is a real recoverable world block; any player can dig it up.
  • Torches, ladders, flares, dynamite, storage crates, outposts, and insurance extend range or soften risk.

Meta layerEconomy and progression

  • Cash upgrades shovel speed and backpack capacity first, then light, traversal, safety, and infrastructure.
  • Job signs issue three-contract sets; completion pays a bonus and increases corporate rank.
  • Promotion gates dynamite clearance, while deployed storage/outposts shorten future return trips.
  • Profiles retain lifetime output and graves; world codes and recruiting links create lightweight social coordination.
  • The global block counter makes every sale and tunnel part of a communal long-horizon objective.

Required screen and interface inventory

Landing page and impossible planetary mandate
Company Report, Damage Map, server counters, profiles, and leaderboards
Employee name, world code, and claim-code registration
First-person voxel shift with funds, depth, capacity, site population, personal/global output
Hotbar, torches, ladders, graves, signs, and other player traces
Employee Handbook and Personnel File
Pack-full / store-locked surface guidance
Company Store with sell and equipment categories
Death, burial receipt, grave coordinates, and respawn

Minimum useful data model

  • VoxelChunk: block material, HP, world position, removal state, placed object or grave payload, persistence version.
  • EmployeeProfile: claim code, name, cash, rank, lifetime blocks, contracts, graves, equipment entitlement.
  • ShiftState: site/world code, spawn permit, inventory, backpack contents, depth, selected hotbar slot, active insurance.
  • MaterialDefinition: depth distribution, durability, sale value, visual/audio treatment.
  • WorldObject: torch, ladder, flare, dynamite charge, storage crate, outpost, grave, job sign; owner and persistence policy.
  • Server aggregates: remaining blocks, shifts, employees, active sites, leaderboards, damage-map tiles.

06
Production sequence

Build the causal loop before the content surface

A practical implementation order for reproducing the observed promise while keeping the prototype testable at every step.

  1. Build authoritative voxel removal, chunk persistence, material drops, capacity, and a local dig–sell–upgrade loop.
  2. Add multiplayer replication, site/world codes, durable tunnels, and placed lights/ladders.
  3. Add death, public graves, recovery coordinates, equipment loss, and one-use insurance.
  4. Add contracts, corporate ranks, dynamite clearance, storage/outposts, profiles, and global counters.
  5. Stress-test chunk concurrency, idempotent rewards, claim-code recovery, exploits, griefing, and world backup/compaction.

Boundaries and unresolved behaviour

Do not encode these as facts yet.
  • Exact server architecture, chunk ownership, anti-cheat, rollback, and concurrent dig resolution are not visible from the client.
  • Complete contract tables, promotion thresholds, dynamite economics, insurance premiums, and outpost rules need deeper play.
  • The session did not verify cross-device claim restoration or coordinated friend entry with a world code.
